input:
## Start-up

Before any attempt is made to pressurise the system, it is essential to confirm that the valve which has been fitted is in fact the correct valve for the protected system, that the inlet and the outlet have been connected in the correct orientation, and that any gag, blank or transport restraint which may have been fitted for the purposes of shipment has been completely removed. It should be clearly understood that a relief valve which leaves the factory in a gagged condition affords no protection whatsoever, and this particular check should always be carried out by direct visual inspection at the valve itself rather than by reference to the accompanying paperwork. The inlet isolation valve should be opened fully, and it should be confirmed that the outlet path is open along the whole of its length, in the sense that the discharge line must be entirely free to its outlet, with no closed valve, blank or other obstruction situated anywhere between the relief valve and the point of discharge. Any liquid which may be standing in the inlet leg or in the discharge line should be drained away, since a slug of liquid in front of the valve can delay the lift, while a slug in the discharge line can give rise to back pressure which the setting does not allow for. The protected system should then be pressurised slowly and carefully. As the pressure rises, the valve should be observed closely: the seat should remain tight, with no audible leakage and no discharge at the outlet. The pressure at which any leakage begins should be noted, and any leakage occurring below the normal operating pressure should be reported before the system is put into service, since a valve which leaks on start-up will rarely seal itself at a later stage. Once the system has reached its normal operating pressure, the pressure, the state of the valve and the condition of the discharge line should be recorded in the operating log, and this record will serve as the baseline against which all subsequent inspections are compared.

## Normal operation

During normal operation, the valve remains shut. The protected system operates below the set pressure, the valve lifts only if that pressure is actually reached, and no action is required on the part of the operator for as long as the system pressure remains within its normal range. The inlet isolation valve should be kept fully open, and locked or sealed in that position where the installation provides for this to be done, since a partly closed inlet valve starves the relief valve and the protection is effectively lost before the valve itself is even reached. The discharge path should be kept in exactly the state in which it was left at start-up, namely open, drained and unobstructed. The valve should be inspected at the intervals laid down in the site schedule: leakage at the seat should be looked for, as shown by discharge at the outlet or by a warm discharge line; corrosion, damage and deposits should be looked for at the inlet and around the spring; and it should be confirmed that no gag, wire or restraint has been refitted in the course of other work. The valve should not be lifted by hand as a routine check unless this is specifically called for by the site procedure, because a manual lift can leave debris on the seat, and a valve which sealed satisfactorily before the lift may not seal after it. Any lift, however brief, should be reported in the operating log, together with the pressure reached and the apparent cause. A lift is the valve doing its work, and it is also evidence that the protected system reached its set pressure, which the operation of the system will need to explain.

## Alarms

There are two alarms which concern this valve. Each alarm is set out below together with the operator action which belongs to it, and it should be noted that no other alarm is raised on the valve itself.

Alarm: inlet pressure rising through the set pressure with no lift from the valve. This means that the protected system has reached the pressure at which the valve must open, and the valve has not in fact opened. Immediate action is called for: the pressure should be reduced at its source by cutting whatever is driving it, whether this is the feed, the heating or the compression, according to what the system provides. If the pressure nevertheless continues to rise, the protected system should be shut down and isolated. The valve must not be gagged, the discharge line must not be stood on, and no attempt should be made to free the valve while it remains under pressure. A valve which has failed to lift is to be removed and bench-tested before the system is returned to service, and the failure is to be recorded together with the pressure reached and the time at which the condition was observed.

Alarm: leakage past the seat during normal operation, as shown by a continuous discharge at the outlet, by sound at the valve, or by a discharge line which remains warm while the system pressure is within its normal range. The leakage should be recorded and reported within the same shift. The valve should be monitored thereafter: a leak which grows, or a leak accompanied by vibration, should be reported again as a changed condition. The valve should be left in service and the discharge path left open; the outlet must never be blanked, plugged or valved off in an attempt to stop the loss, because a blanked outlet removes the protection on which the system depends. The valve will be removed for seat repair at the next shutdown of the protected system, or earlier if the leakage grows to the point where the loss itself becomes the operating problem.

## Shutdown

The protected system should be shut down by its own procedure, and the pressure should be allowed to fall in a controlled manner. The relief valve is not a vent: it should not be used to depressurise the system, and it should not be held open by hand against a falling pressure. When the system pressure has fallen to a safe level and the system is at rest, the inlet isolation valve should be closed, and it should then be proved, by means of the drain or vent provided by the installation, that the section between the isolation valve and the relief valve has been fully depressurised. Only at that point should the valve be touched. If the valve is to be removed, the inlet leg should be drained, the joints broken in the order set out in the site procedure, and the open connections left behind by the system capped or blanked. The valve should be tagged with its identity and with the reason for its removal, and the removal, the condition found and the state of the seat should be recorded in the operating log. A valve which has been removed after a lift, after a failure to lift, or after a period of leakage is to be sent for bench testing before it is refitted or replaced, while a valve removed in a routine shutdown is returned to service only after the inspection laid down in the site schedule has been carried out. On refitting, the start-up section of this chapter applies in full.

The chapter closes where the next start-up begins: a protected system returns to service with a valve whose condition is recorded, whose discharge path is open, and whose last test or inspection stands on record.
